title: Sequential Sorting
body:
Sorting on one processor, one comparison at a time. "Sequential" is there to distinguish it
from the parallel chapter: the sorting networks and mesh sorts that do many comparisons at
once. The algorithms themselves are the ones [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] teaches, and they own
their own notes: [[Bubble Sort]], [[Insertion Sort]], [[Merge Sort]], [[Quick Sort]], plus
heapsort inside [[Heap]]. This note is the map over them and the one argument none of them
carry: **why $n \log n$ is a wall.**

## The map

| Sort | Average | Worst | Space | Stable | Use it when |
|---|---|---|---|:-:|---|
| [[Bubble Sort]] | $O(n^2)$ | $O(n^2)$ | $O(1)$ | yes | never, it is a teaching example |
| [[Insertion Sort]] | $O(n^2)$ | $O(n^2)$ | $O(1)$ | yes | $n$ is tiny, or the data is nearly sorted |
| heapsort ([[Heap]]) | $O(n \log n)$ | $O(n \log n)$ | $O(1)$ | no | you need the guarantee *and* the space |
| [[Merge Sort]] | $O(n \log n)$ | $O(n \log n)$ | $O(n)$ | yes | [[Linked List]]s, external sorting, stability matters |
| [[Quick Sort]] | $O(n \log n)$ | $O(n^2)$ | $O(\log n)$ | no | the default for arrays in memory |

The quadratic pair and the linearithmic pair differ by *what they exploit*. Insertion sort
does work proportional to how out-of-order the input is, so it is $O(n)$ on sorted data;
merge sort does its $\log n$ levels regardless and cannot be beaten by a friendly input. That
is why real library sorts are hybrids: [[Quick Sort]] down to small partitions, then
[[Insertion Sort]] to finish, with a heapsort escape hatch if the recursion goes too deep.

## Why no comparison sort beats $n \log n$

The parent's Core Facts state this; here is the argument. A comparison sort learns about the
input only by asking "is $a_i < a_j$?", so its whole execution is a binary **decision tree**:
each internal node a comparison, each branch an answer, each leaf one final ordering.

- There are $n!$ possible orderings, and the algorithm has to be able to output every one, so
  the tree needs at least $n!$ leaves.
- A binary tree with $L$ leaves has height at least $\log_2 L$.
- The worst-case number of comparisons is the height, so it is at least $\log_2(n!)$.
- Stirling gives $\log_2(n!) = \Theta(n \log n)$.

So $\Omega(n \log n)$ comparisons, for *any* comparison sort, no cleverness admitted. Merge
sort and heapsort hit that bound, which makes them asymptotically optimal. The $n!$ comes
straight from [[Permutation]]: counting the search space before searching it, again.

The catch in the premise is the way out. The bound only binds algorithms that use
comparisons. Counting sort, radix sort, and bucket sort look at the *values* instead (digit
by digit, or as array indices) and run in $O(n)$ or $O(nk)$, at the cost of only working on
keys with the right structure, usually bounded integers. None of them has a note in the
vault; they belong with [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]].

## What "sequential" is being contrasted with

The book's parallel chapters sort with **comparators** wired in a fixed pattern: a network
that sorts any input in a fixed number of *rounds*, with many independent comparisons per
round. Batcher's odd-even merge sorts $n$ items in $O(\log^2 n)$ rounds, which is impossible
sequentially, because the rounds happen at once rather than one after another. The
$n \log n$ bound above is untouched by this: the total comparison *count* is higher, it is
the wall-clock depth that drops. Same distinction as power versus time in [[Nondeterminism]].

## Core Facts to Know

- A comparison sort's execution is a binary decision tree with at least $n!$ leaves.
- Height $\geq \log_2(n!) = \Theta(n \log n)$, so **no comparison sort beats $O(n \log n)$**.
- [[Merge Sort]] and heapsort meet the bound; [[Quick Sort]] meets it on average only.
- Counting, radix, and bucket sort dodge the bound by not comparing; they need structured keys.
- **Stable** means equal elements keep their original relative order. Merge, insertion, and
  bubble are stable; quicksort and heapsort are not.
- Nearly-sorted input is $O(n)$ for [[Insertion Sort]] and no faster for [[Merge Sort]].
- Sorting networks trade total comparisons for depth, and are not bound by the sequential
  argument in wall-clock terms.
